Your projects

Stored only in this browser, on this device. Use Export in Setup & Backup to move a project to another device or keep a backup copy.

Tap a story and it loads straight away — there is no second step. Tap the button again, or anywhere else, to close this without loading anything. Project overview

Filled in vs. still blank, phase by phase. Tap any phase to work on it.

Intake — premise first

Premise, key question, theme, and characters' questions.

Length

Length matters when it is a real constraint — a challenge limit, a book contract, a form you have chosen. Set the one target; the budget and scale it implies are summarised in one line, with the detail behind a tap.

Worldbuilding

The world behind the story. Build only what a scene or arc actually needs — sections another scene needs are listed first, and each section says what it is for before you open it.

Characters

Write these before you expand the synopsis.

Story Arcs — arcs & Seven-Point beats

Every arc gets its own Seven-Point map (Dan Wells): build backwards — Resolution first, then Hook, Midpoint, Turns, Pinches.

Scenes

Skeleton only — no prose is written here. When a scene is ready, use its copy button to paste a ready-to-write sheet into your prose editor.

Visual map — arcs × scenes

Arcs are rows, scenes are columns. Tap + to tag a beat. On mobile you scroll sideways through scenes; on larger screens you get the full grid.

Scene list

What counts as a scene? List every scene you want to write, in order — a scene has its own Goal → Conflict → Disaster. Quiet beats and lovely passages live inside the scene they belong to; give something its own card only when it has its own goal, conflict and disaster.

Readiness check — before you draft

One check, after planning and before writing prose: does every part of the plan actually have what drafting will need? Everything here is read from your own plan — and most of it is fixed right here: tap “Edit here” on a row and write into the plan without leaving this page. The page link stays for the few things that need their full editor. Planning gaps found later, in Editing, are too late to fix cheaply; that is why they live here and not in the Structural pass.

Editing — big to small

One kind of edit at a time, in this order. You draft in your prose editor — this page is the diagnostic pass over that draft, not a second draft.

How to use these passes

One lens at a time, big to small. The ⓘ beside each pass title carries that pass's full guidance.

Setup & Backup

This tool is one self-contained web page. No server, no account, nothing you type leaves the device unless you export it yourself.

Back up & move projects

Projects save automatically in this browser's storage on this device only — clearing browser data or using a private tab can erase them, so export regularly.

On mobile and larger screens, Export opens the share sheet — tap Save to Files and choose a folder (for example iCloud Drive or On My Device). The file is named like your-project-20261101-0930.json — project name, date, and time — so searching Files for “json” finds it, and saving again later the same day makes a new file instead of overwriting the earlier one. If you close the share sheet without saving, no file is saved. Where file sharing isn't available, Export starts a download instead — look in Files › Downloads. Move a project: Export on one device → save the file to Files / iCloud Drive → open this tool on the other device → Import. Importing never overwrites: a project with the same name arrives as a copy.

Reference sheets for your prose editor

This tool holds the skeleton only — there is no prose field. Draft prose in whatever editor you write in. The quickest route while drafting is per scene: open the scene in Scenes and tap Copy for your prose editor, then paste into a new note or document there — POV, what must happen, feeling, beat tags, the Scene & Sequel decision, and the [bracketed] stage instructions are laid out with a blank prose space underneath, so you can start writing immediately, deleting the brackets or keeping them above the prose. The copy also carries a rich-text version with the bracketed lines highlighted yellow — your editor may keep that highlight when you paste; the brackets and blank lines between them always come through, the yellow is best-effort. For the whole project at once, use one of these Markdown sheets for the current project. Both open the same share sheet / download flow as the JSON exports above.

Overall story sheet — one sheet for the whole story: premise, key question, theme, framing, characters, the Seven-Point map, then every scene in order.

Scene sheets — one section per scene to copy into its own note or document in your prose editor. Stage instructions are written one per line; each line appears in its own [brackets] with a blank line between lines, and a blank space underneath for your prose, so you can delete the brackets or keep them above the prose. Copy finished scenes together, in scene order, in your prose editor, then paste them into your publishing tool.

What is a .md file? “.md” is Markdown — a plain-text file with simple marks for headings and bold (like # Title). It is not a story file and not the JSON backup above. Its purpose is reading: a readable reference sheet of your whole story plan, and per-scene sheets ready to copy into your prose editor to write from. It opens and reads fine on mobile and larger screens — in the Files preview, Notes, or any text app — no special app needed. If you'd rather skip Markdown entirely, use the .txt versions instead: exactly the same words, saved as plain text that opens anywhere.

Scenes appear in both sheets in plain scene order — the order you arrange them in Scenes is the order they are assembled in.

Use it like an app — on mobile or a larger screen

  1. Open this page in Safari on your device.
  2. Tap the Share button (square with an arrow pointing up).
  3. Scroll and tap Add to Home Screen, then Add.
  4. It now opens full-screen from its own icon, and works offline once loaded. Your projects stay in that device's browser storage — Export a backup before switching devices or clearing Safari data.

Works offline — planes included

This tool is client-side only: it makes no server calls, needs no account, and everything you type is saved in this browser on this device. Once the page has loaded, editing, saving, and Export (share sheet / Save to Files) all work with no connection — including in airplane mode.

  1. Open the site once while online so the whole page loads.
  2. Add it to your Home Screen (Share → Add to Home Screen) and open it from that icon.
  3. After that it opens and works offline — write on the plane, export when you land.

About service workers: this tool ships as a single self-contained HTML file, so it can't install a separate service-worker file; the home-screen copy iOS keeps after an online load is what makes offline work. If a fresh offline load ever fails, connect once, reopen the site online, then reopen it from the home-screen icon — that refreshes the copy. Your projects are never uploaded anywhere; they only move when you Export them yourself.

Host your own copy (optional)

You only need this if you want your own web address for the tool, reachable from any device without Muse. The tool is a single index.html file — ask for the exported HTML file of this page, then pick either host:

Easiest — Netlify Drop (no account setup up front, ~2 minutes):

  1. On a computer, put the index.html file in a new folder (any name).
  2. Go to app.netlify.com/drop and drag the folder onto the page.
  3. Netlify gives you a web address (like your-name.netlify.app). Open it on any device, then Add to Home Screen as above. Create a free Netlify account to claim and keep the address.
  4. To update the tool later, drag the new folder onto the same site in your Netlify dashboard.

GitHub Pages (free, if you already use GitHub):

  1. Create a new public repository, e.g. writing-tool.
  2. Upload index.html to the repository (Add file → Upload files).
  3. In the repo: Settings → Pages → Source: “Deploy from a branch”, branch main, folder / (root) → Save.
  4. After a minute your tool is at https://your-username.github.io/writing-tool/.

Either way, hosting only serves the empty tool — your stories are never uploaded. They live in each device's browser storage until you Export them yourself.

The systems behind this tool

  • Seven-Point Structure — Dan Wells (LTUE / Writing Excuses), adapted from the Star Trek Roleplaying Game Narrator's Guide.
  • Scene & Sequel — Dwight V. Swain, Techniques of the Selling Writer (1965).
  • Snowflake Method — Randy Ingermanson: sentence → paragraph → character summaries → synopsis → scene list.
  • Hero's Journey — used here only as an arc check on Seven-Point, never as a second outline.
  • Want / Need & self-revelation — John Truby, The Anatomy of Story: the want drives the plot; the need is what the ending answers.
  • Causality — beats should connect with “but” or “therefore”, never “and then” (Matt Stone & Trey Parker): if two beats can swap places without breaking anything, one of them is not doing causal work.
  • Worldbuilding — Brandon Sanderson's Laws: understood systems can solve problems, mysterious ones can only cause them; limitations matter more than powers; expand what you have before adding new.
